Rung by the local band with the bells half muffled to mark the anniversary of the death of The Right Honourable Frederick John Robinson, first Earl of Ripon, who died on 28th January 1859.

Lord Ripon lived at Nocton Hall and owned the Nocton Estate. All Saints Church was built as a memorial to Lord Ripon and the peal of six bells were given by his wife Lady Sarah Albinia Louisa, Countess of Ripon in 1865 in memory of him.
He was a former Chancellor of the Exchequer as well as a former Prime Minster, and is buried in the family vault here under All Saints.

Rung at the Civic Church by the Civic Ringers whilst a vigil was taking place across from St Mary’s on the Brayford waterfront marking the first anniversary of the invasion of Ukrainian. Rung to show our solidarity with all Ukrainians but also praying for Peace & Freedom.

St Mary le Wigford is home to the Lincoln Ukrainian Cultural Center, which has been set up in this Church and the adjoining Church Hall for Ukrainians in the City and surrounding areas, giving them a place to meet and to be Ukrainian together, eat Ukrainian food, enjoy Ukrainian culture and friendship - We regard St Mary's as Ukrainian on Sunday's when they meet! The Church is theirs, its their home, its a little bit of Ukraine and they can do things their way!

Yesterday evening on the eve of the first anniversary  ITV Calendar News broadcast its 6pm news live from St Mary’s for 30 minutes with the members of the Lincoln Ukrainian Cultural Center who call this home. The programme was focused all about Ukraine and how Lincoln has been involved in helping and supporting the Ukrainians.

The Annual Culfrey Ringing.

Rung on the back three (the original three) on Lady Day to mark the end of the ringing of the Culfrey Bell (the tenor) each evening at 7pm between Michaelmas Day & Lady Day, a local tradition dating back to the seventeenth century to help guide lost travellers off the heath to the safety of the village.
The bells were rung up to 7pm, after which the Culfrey Bell (the tenor) was rung for 10 mins.

The Culfrey Trust still provide new bell ropes for the Culfrey Bell, upkeep the Church clock which took over the ringing of the bell, and provide two bungalows for elder parishioners called the Culfrey Bungalows on the site of the old Culfrey Cottages.

Rung as part of the national ringing at 8pm across the Commonwealth to mark the 10th anniversary of the signing of the Commonwealth of Nations Charter, by the late Queen, Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II.
To represent Queen's we decided to ring a touch of 135 changes followed by a touch of 246 changes.

It was intended that this ringing would take place earlier today at 11am to coincide with the flag raising ceremony at the City Guildhall, just up the High Street from St Mary's, which was to be attended by His Majesty’s Lord-Lieutenant for the County of Lincolnshire, the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln, the City Sheriff and members of the Civic Party as part of the 73 City's across the UK raising the new Commonwealth of Nations Flag of Peace at 11am, however this was sadly cancelled at the last minute due to the high winds and the fact the flag had to be raised from on top of the roof of the Guildhall.

The Mayor and Civic Party were pleased to know that the Civic Bells would still be rung today but instead at 8pm even though this morning's ceremony had to be cancelled and hence Lincoln was being represented.

The Civic Bells pealed out over the City during the Freedom Parade of RAF Waddington, as they exercised their right to parade/march through the City of Lincoln with Colours flying, bayonets fixed, bands playing and bells pealing. Marking the bases close connections to the City standing immediately to the south of the City.

Lincoln is proud of its close connections with the RAF and looks forward to celebrating the 80th anniversary of the Dambusters Raid in a few weeks time which took off from RAF Scampton immediately to the north of the City. RAF Scampton also held the Freedom of the City (14th May 1993) and in past years have taken part in this joint Freedom Parade for both bases, but sadly Scampton was closed at the end of 2022 which saw their final Freedom Parade last year. This year would have been their 30th anniversary of being granted the Freedom of the City of Lincoln.
Today’s Freedom Parade saw 150 personnel from RAF Waddington marching through the City to mark the granting of the Freedom of the City of Lincoln to RAF Waddington on 25th April 1959.

The parade was led by the RAF Waddington Pipes and Drums and preceded by the Civic Procession which took place from the Guildhall down the High Street to the City War Memorial to wait for the parade to arrive.

The parade marched down the High Street from St Martin’s Square, passing the Guildhall to the City War Memorial, which stands 150 yards away from the Civic Church of St Mary le Wigford and within earshot of the bells, from where the bells could be clear heard pealing out over the parade. The parade came to a halt at the City War Memorial and a flypast took place.

The parade was inspected by the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln, Councillor Rosanne Kirk. Also present were the City Sheriff, members of the City of Lincoln Civic Party, the Freemen of the City and other City Dignitaries including the MP for Lincoln. The official salute to the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln was given before the Parade marched off to finish in City Square.

Rung to remind the general public & shoppers in the City centre of the importance of today. It is felt strongly that the bells should be rung and heard today in this ever secular and modern world that we live in, to remind everyone that today is a special day.

Rung on the eightieth anniversary of Operation Chastise, AKA the Dambusters Raid, when 617 Squadron RAF Bomber Command successfully destroyed two German dams in the Ruhr valley, hastening a return to peace in Europe.

Specially arranged and rung with the bells half muffled in ‘Bomber County’ to commemorate the 80th anniversary of the famous ‘Dambusters Raid’ which took place 16th/17th May 1943, on the Ruhr Valley Dams by 617 Squadron which was based at and flew from neighbouring RAF Scampton.
Rung remembering the 133 airmen who participated in this daring raid, but especially the 53 aircrew who were killed during the raid and did not return.
Lincoln has strong links with the RAF, with RAF Scampton based just north of the City, being granted the honour of the Freedom of the City in 1993.
The sight of Lincoln Cathedral for returning pilots and crews has always been a welcome sight symbolising they had returned safe and were back home!

Rung also remembering especially “Barnes Wallis” who came up with the concept and developed the bouncing bombs used in the raid. “Wing Commander Guy Gibson”, Commanding Officer of 617 Squadron who led the raid and finally “Nigger”, Guy Gibson’s black labrador retriever who was the mascot of 617 Squadron. Nigger died on the morning of the Dambusters Raid, 16th May 1943, when he was hit by a car outside RAF Scampton. Nigger was buried at RAF Scampton at midnight at the request of Gibson whilst he was leading the raid, and where his grave still remains.

St Mary-le-Wigford Church can be seen from the International Bomber Command Memorial, which is built on top of Canwick Hill overlooking the City of Lincoln and its Cathedral (a symbol to the aircrews they had returned home and safe). We are very proud here in Lincolnshire of the Dambusters and Bomber Command!

Per Dominum.
Amen.
V: O Lord, save Charles our King
R: And hear us in the day when we call upon thee.
Let us pray.

We beseech thee, almighty God, that thy servant Charles our King, who by thy mercy hath undertaken the government of this realm, may advance in all virtues; that being meetly adorned therewith, he may be able to avoid the enormity of sin and to come well-pleasing to thee, who art the way, the truth, and the life. Through our Lord.

It was successfully lowered, sent away for restoration by Taylor’s of Loughborough, and reinstated successfully by them. Full details of the bell are documented on our website at:

Half muffled general ringing in memory of Tom Freeston who died on 6th June 2023 by  members of the Boston area group and the Lincoln Diocesan Guild.

Tom learned  to ring at Boston in 1946. He became tower captain and rang there over 9 decades- last climbing the 200 steps to the ringing room at the age of 86, when building works at the church stopped the ringing for a while.
Tom was a former president of the Eastern branch of the Lincoln Diocesan Guild and had many friends throughout the guild.

We would like to associate the ringing today with those ringers who could not attend due to prior engagements, wedding ringing, the Ridgeman trophy , and the steps to the ringing room! The many tributes received are a testament to the gentleman Tom was . Rest in peace.

Ringing to mark The Millennial Anniversary of The Translation of St. Alfege's body from St Paul's Cathedral to Canterbury Cathedral in June 1023. St Alfege, Archbishop of Canterbury, was martyred on the site of St Alfege's Church Greenwich in 1012 and his body was initially taken to St Paul's. King Cnut ordered that St Alfege's body should be reburied at Canterbury, where he now rests behind the High Altar.

Rung after we attended The Eucharist at St Paul's Cathedral at 1230pm, having done service ringing at St Vedast Foster Lane beforehand. After the service, several parishioners from St Alfege's did a pilgrimage walk to Greenwich. The ringers then continued celebrations with ringing at St James Garlickhythe and St Magnus the Martyr and finally ringing at Greenwich to welcome the pilgrims back.

On the back 5 of the chime of 8 bells, on Father’s Day prior to Morning Service. In remembrance of Simon D Ellis, late husband of Kate Ellis, who met a tragic death on May 8th and whose funeral was on June 14th. The chimer taught Kate to ring up to a standard of ringing at least one Quarter Peal before she left Ecclesfield School, and then, taken up with work, marriage to Simon, and two daughters, she gave up ringing only to return in November 2022 to join the newly revived team at St Leonard’s, Wortley under the tutorship of Andrew and Lynn Beevers, of St Mary’s Ecclesfield, and by May, rang in Coronation celebrations. Simon’s tragic loss, at the end of the three-day coronation celebrations was mentioned in the funeral service in Thurgoland Parish Church by the officiating priest, who blessed his very active life of kindness and love. “Rest in Peace in the Lord’s presence.”

After the Quarter Peal, the hymns from the funeral were chimed in the bells: Crimond (The Lord is My Shepherd), Mannheim (Lead us, Heavenly Father, Lead us) and Eventide (Abide with Me) before the service began.

To celebrate fifty years since Michael Henshaw's first bellringing lesson at Fyfield, Essex on 2nd July 1973. Remembering, with gratitude, Stan Clark (1903-1994) and Roger Burberry (1946-2005) who taught him to ring.

Leaving church on Sunday morning, Mr. Clark asked "how old are you, Michael?" "Twelve? Then it is about time for you to learn to ring. Come to the bell tower tomorrow at 7:30". There was no question of not complying. It led to fifty years of meeting great people, attempting great challenges, and having great fun. I am grateful that bellringing has shaped so much of my life and led to so many friendships.
Michael was Ringing Master at Kirk Ella for sixteen years during the 1980s and 90s.

To celebrate the lives and service of the four Chavasse brothers, sons of Francis Chavasse, Bishop of Liverpool all of whom served with distinction in the Ypres Salient during the Great War between them winning two Victoria Crosses, three Military Crosses and a Croix de Guerre.

[Christopher Chavasse was awarded the Military Cross and the Croix de Guerre. He survived the war to become Bishop of Rochester and the founding Master of St Peter’s College Oxford. His younger twin Noel trained in Oxford and Liverpool as an orthopaedic surgeon and served with the RAMC. He won the Military Cross and was the only person to have been awarded the Victoria Cross twice during the Great War. Both twins had represented their country in the 1908 Olympic Games. The third brother Bernard also served as a military surgeon in the War and was awarded the Military Cross. He went on to become a leading ophthalmologist after the war. Aidan’s plans to train for the priesthood were interrupted by the outbreak of war. Considered by his superiors to be the bravest man in his brigade but was lost after an attack on Sanctuary Wood in July 1917. Aidan’s body was never found despite Bernard having gone three times into no man’s land to try to find him. He is remembered on the Menin Gate. A month later Noel was awarded his second VC for his bravery in recovering and treating wounded colleagues even when wounded himself. He succumbed to his wounds on August 4th 1917.

Given the impact of the two surviving brothers we can only imagine the potential contributions of the brothers who were lost to the madness of war. May they all Rest in Peace and Live on in Eternal Glory.]

Rung half muffled to remember the life of Derrick McRobert who died in his sleep on Wednesday 2nd August aged 77. The evening before his death he attended the usual practice at St John's, and socialised afterwards in the Cross Keys.

Derrick had been a ringer at St John's for over 25 years, had rung over 100 QP's on the bells and 1 peal. He was the Tower archivist, very keen on the history of ringing in the town. He was a unique personality and a great raconteur and an absolute mine of information about so many diverse subjects. A man of generosity and a friend to all.
Grandsire Doubles was his favourite method, often calling it from the 3rd.

Chris Grundy, Sarah Mattock, Tim Richards, Alun Davies, Mike Daybell, PaulBest, Sue Hucknall, Christine Leech, John Burnup, Bill Todd and Peter Cox and many others wish to be associated with this ringing.  RIP

Rung on the back three (the original three) on Michaelmas Day to mark the start of the ringing of the Culfrey Bell (the tenor) each evening at 7pm between Michaelmas Day & Lady Day, a local tradition dating back to the seventeenth century to help guide lost travellers off the heath to the safety of the village.
The bells were rung up to 7pm, after which the Culfrey Bell (the tenor) was rung for 10 mins.

The Culfrey Trust still provide new bell ropes for the Culfrey Bell, upkeep the Church clock which took over the ringing of the bell, and provide two bungalows for elder parishioners called the Culfrey Bungalows on the site of the old Culfrey Cottages.

Rung open in celebration of the life of Doreen Ashton, immediately prior to her funeral here at this Church, the Church where she married her beloved George 71 years ago.

Doreen was highly respected within Lincoln, volunteering for various things across the City, but especially in connection to Lincoln City Football Club 'The Imps', and the Lincoln Branch of the Conservative Association, as well as her involvement in the Civic Church of St Mary-le-Wigford where she supported her husband George who was Church Warden.

Doreen for many decades undertook the catering at Lincoln City Football Club and her cheese and onion rolls were renowned by fans. She also undertook catering on the coaches for the away matches. Doreen and her husband George can trace their links to attending and supporting the Imps since the 1930's and have been avid supporters ever since. She is a legend in her own right and is affectionately thought of as the grandmother of the Imps!

Whilst we were ringing the funeral cortege did a lap of Sincil Bank (home of the Imps) where fans and staff made a guard of honour before it made its way the short distance to the Church which was full to capacity with many Imps fans.

Doreen was also a loyal supporter of the Civic Church in Lincoln, St Mary-le-Wigford, and she supported her husband George who was Church Warden there for many decades, tirelessly keeping St Mary's open and functioning.
Doreen sadly passed away on 1st September 2023 aged 91. RIP Doreen.

Rounds rung following the Election of Bishop Philip Mounstephen as Bishop of Winchester during the singing of the Te Deum by the choir, thus reviving a 700 year old tradition. On 28 September 1334, when news reached the monks at St Swithun’s Priory, that their bishop, Adam of Orlton, had been ‘restored to his temporalities’ by Edward III, they were instructed ‘to assemble in the church, ring the bells, and sing a solemn Te Deum to the accompaniment of organs…’.  Ringers from three local towers in the Diocesan Guild took part.

Rung half-muffled in memory of Stan Smith, member of the congregation for over 50 years and stalwart of the community.

Stan was born in Birkenhead in 1933 and the family moved into Liverpool shortly after where he became a chorister at Pier Head, witnessing the destruction of the Church during World War II. After the war he completed National Service in the RAF and then began training for Ordination but dropped out of Theological College to study instead for the new profession of Social Work, initially in Liverpool and then Southampton. He worked in Leeds and then moved with his wife Phoebe and two children to Wylam in 1972 to work in Newcastle. More recently in the last decade he remained active with his local branch of the British Association of Social Workers, despite having retired some years ago.

Rung on ‘Arnhem Sunday’ prior to the Arnhem Service attended by 216 Parachute Signal Squadron, marking the 79th anniversary of Operation Market Garden 17th – 26th September 1944, and in particular the Battle of Arnhem where the 1st Airborne Divisional Signals tried to secure a bridgehead over the River Rhine.
Especially remembering the 27 members of the 1st Airborne Divisional Signals who were billeted at Caythorpe and who did not return from Arnhem.
Caythorpe has close connections to Arnhem, during the Second World War the 1st Airborne Divisional Signals were based at Caythorpe.

To this day Caythorpe maintains close links with 216 Parachute Signal Squadron, who consider Caythorpe to be their spiritual home and St Vincent’s as their Regimental Church. The North Aisle of the Church is named and dedicated ‘The Arnhem Aisle’ and holds the two Regimental Memorial Windows, the Arnham Memorial, the Books of Remembrance and Regimental Memorials for conflicts since 1945 up to the present day.

Every year at the start of September Caythorpe holds the ‘Arnhem Weekend’ which begins with the Village Gala on the Saturday which includes among other things the tug-of-war and football match between the villagers and the Paras. On the Saturday evening the Regimental Dinner is held and on the Sunday there is the Parade through the village of 216 Parachute Signal Squadron along with the Veterans to St Vincent’s for the memorial service.

This quarter peal was rung in memory of Robert (Bob) Churchill, who passed away on the 25th October, aged 97.

I’d like to say a big thank you to the band. Considering we mostly consisted of 6 bell ringers, I think we did incredibly well. There was some very nice striking, and a first for David on 8 – congratulations! Bob would’ve appreciated this the most.
A bit about Bob:
Bob was a long standing member of our association, who was until recent years, tower captain of Husborne Crawley, and Eversholt.

I first met Bob at Husborne Crawley almost 10 years ago, when I turned up as an eager youngster who could just about handle a bell on my own. Being old school, Bob chucked me in at the deep end with bell ringing jargon, and learning methods, but it is an environment I thrived in, and thoroughly enjoyed.
A few years later, Bob introduced me to the bells of Eversholt. A heavy 6, that were incredibly hard going, with their 100 year old egg-shaped ball bearings, and similar shaped wheels to match.

These bells were in my opinion, the bells closest to Bob’s heart. Most of his later life was dedicated to getting them restored, with fundraising that included bike rides, and selling his poetry books (volumes 3 and 4). Once restored, Bob was in his 90s. However, this didn’t stop him training up a new band of ringers – incredible.
Throughout his life, Bob likely taught countless people how to ring. I was lucky to be one of them, and he certainly made me the ringer I am today.
Thank you Bob.

In 1434, a local knight, Sir Thomas de Soothill, flew into a rage upon hearing that a servant boy had failed to attend church that week. He grabbed the boy and, lifting him up, threw him into a mill pond, where the boy drowned. Overwhelmed by remorse at the murder, and as an act of penance, de Soothill paid for a new 1300-weight tenor bell for the parish church (now Dewsbury Minster), asking for it to be tolled at his funeral as people prayed for his soul. Sir Thomas also instituted the practice that the bell (named Black Tom after its benefactor) should be to be rung on Christmas Eve, with one toll for each year of the Christian Era, to proclaim the defeat of evil and the forgiveness of all sins, not just his own.
